Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 78
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Database Administrator
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Threat: Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe

Vignette:
For seventy-eight years, Thomas had considered himself a man who understood systems. As a database administrator, he spent his days imposing order on chaos, structuring information so that it made sense, so that it could be queried and predicted. Nothing in his long career had prepared him for the way his own body would betray him. The event itself had been unremarkable in its onset—a routine physical, a slightly elevated white blood cell count, a referral he had not taken seriously until the word "leukemia" appeared in the specialist's notes. What Thomas remembered most vividly now, two years after successful treatment, was not the chemotherapy or the hospital stays but a single afternoon in the infusion center. The room had been too cold, and someone in the next chair had been eating a tuna sandwich. That smell—tuna fish, metallic and insistent—had woven itself into the moments when the nurse had checked his port, when he had watched the clear fluid begin its slow drip into his arm, when he had understood with absolute certainty that he might not walk out of this room. He could smell it now, writing this, as if the woman were sitting beside him. That was what frightened him most: the memories did not behave like memories. They felt more real than the chair he was sitting in. When they came, he was back in that cold room, the fear as fresh as the day it had first arrived.

Thomas had divorced twenty years ago and lived alone in a modest suburban house. He had always taken pride in his independence, in the quiet order of his routines. But after the illness, something shifted. He began to notice that he could not relax inside his own home. The front door was locked three times before bed. He found himself standing at the living room window at odd hours, scanning the street for nothing in particular. He was certain, though he could not explain why, that danger could find him anywhere. The world had become a dangerous place, and his body kept reacting as if the threat were still present—muscles tight, heart accelerating at the sound of a car door, at the creak of a floorboard. He had lost his faith in the basic decency of things. People, life, a higher power—it all felt like a structure that had collapsed. He had nothing to query anymore.

The consequences crept in slowly. At work, he had always been reliable, but now he found himself unable to concentrate. The smell of someone's lunch in the breakroom would send him spiraling, and he would retreat to his cubicle, heart pounding, the memory of the infusion center so vivid that he could feel the cold vinyl of the chair against his arms. He started taking his lunch in his car, then eating at his desk with the door closed. His supervisor noticed, commented that he seemed "distracted." Thomas could not explain that he was not distracted—he was too alert, too watchful, too busy scanning for a threat that no one else could see. He began to dread the office potlucks, the communal meals, the way a whiff of canned fish could undo an entire afternoon. He stopped going to the grocery store during lunch hour. He stopped eating out altogether. His social life, already thin, evaporated completely.

What finally brought Thomas to seek help was not the fear itself but the exhaustion. He was seventy-eight years old, and he was tired of being on guard. He had survived the illness, but he had not survived the aftermath. He sat in the therapist's office with his hands folded in his lap, and he said, quietly, "I don't know how to feel safe anymore. I don't know if I ever will." What he hoped for, more than anything, was not to be free of the memory—he knew that was impossible—but to stop living inside it. He wanted the tuna sandwich to just be a tuna sandwich.
